summary: Across two iterations, we improved the 2D knapsack score from 94.46 → 94.84 (hill-climbing over orderings) → 95.21 (simulated annealing over joint ordering × per-item heuristic space). The key discovery in iter-2 is that expanding the search space to include per-item heuristic assignments — not just item orderings — was the actual mechanism for improvement; gap filling contributed zero points.
key_points: Score progression: baseline 94.46 → iter-1 hill-climbing 94.84 (+0.38) → iter-2 SA with per-item heuristics 95.21 (+0.37). Total gain: +0.75 points over two iterations.

The ordering space (M=8-12 types) is small enough that hill-climbing already finds near-optimal orderings. SA over orderings alone matched hill-climbing exactly (94.84). The gain came from jointly optimizing which MaxRects heuristic (BSSF/BAF/BL/BLSF) to use for each item type — a combinatorial dimension hill-climbing didn't explore.

Gap filling (post-hoc insertion into residual free rectangles) provides zero value — the per-item heuristic optimization already achieves space utilization tight enough that no remaining free rectangle can fit any available item. This refutes the hypothesis that sequential ordered packing leaves exploitable waste.

Next iteration should investigate: (a) partial repack / destroy-rebuild moves within SA (remove a placed item type and reinsert others into freed space), (b) look-ahead rotation decisions (currently rotation is decided greedily per placement), (c) multi-pass strip decomposition (split the bin into horizontal/vertical strips optimized independently), or (d) increasing the heuristic vocabulary (e.g., adding worst-fit or contact-perimeter-lite variants) to give SA more levers.

Risk assessment: We're at 95.21/100 with diminishing returns — each iteration gained ~0.37 points. The scoring formula normalizes against a fractional upper bound that ignores geometry, so the last ~5 points may require near-perfect geometric utilization. A next iteration targeting 95.5+ is plausible but gains will likely be smaller.
